chapters.title: Chapter 5: Comparing Markets Like an Investor

lessons.title: Valuations, Earnings Growth, and Sector Mix: US vs Europe vs Asia vs India

children.text: In mid-September 2026, the US 10-year government bond yielded about 5.04% and India's 10-year G-Sec about 7.10%. The S&P 500 traded at about 19 times next year's earnings, Europe's STOXX 600 at about 14.6 times, Japan's TOPIX at about 16 times, and Indian large caps at about 20 times. On those numbers alone, India was one of the most expensive major markets in the world. Does that mean Indian stocks were overpriced and Europe was a bargain? Not necessarily. You have spent four chapters learning how each region works. This lesson gives you five tools to compare them properly, the way a global fund manager does.

body.text: No single number tells you which market is cheap. A proper comparison combines valuation, earnings growth, sector mix, cash returned to shareholders and currency. A market can be expensive and still worth owning, or cheap and still a trap.

A gap of one or two points between markets is within the noise. Large, persistent gaps, like India's premium to emerging markets, are what deserve attention.

The extra return investors expect from shares over a safe government bond, to compensate for the higher risk of owning equities.

body.caption: A simple way to compare the return on shares with the return on safe government bonds

body.title: India's yield gap
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 trades at a trailing P/E of 20.2x, and India's 10-year G-Sec yields 7.10%. What is the yield gap, earnings yield minus bond yield, in percentage points? Round to two decimal places. Enter a negative number if the bond yield is higher.
body.explanation: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ 20.2 × 100 = 4.95%. Yield gap = 4.95% − 7.10% = −2.15 percentage points. For the US, 1 ÷ 19.1 × 100 = 5.24%, minus a 5.04% bond yield gives just +0.20 points. Both gaps are thin, which tells you that investors in both markets are relying on future earnings growth, not today's earnings, to justify current prices.

body.text: A negative yield gap does not mean Indian shares must fall. A bond's coupon is fixed, but company earnings grow. Indian corporate earnings have historically grown faster than those of developed markets, partly because nominal GDP growth and inflation are higher. Indian bond yields are also higher for the same reason. The yield gap is a warning light, not a verdict: it tells you how much growth is already priced in.

children.text: India's valuation premium rests on one argument: faster earnings growth for longer. Short-term estimates jump around. After the fourth quarter of FY26, analysts' estimates for Nifty 50 earnings growth in FY27 ranged from about 15% to 17%, while US earnings were also growing strongly in 2026 on the AI boom. One strong year does not make a trend, so professionals use longer-term growth assumptions when comparing markets. The PEG ratio from Chapter 3 is the simplest way to do it.

body.caption: Growth-adjusted valuation using illustrative long-term earnings growth assumptions

body.title: India's PEG
body.prompt: Using the illustrative table, India trades at about 20x forward earnings with an assumed long-term earnings growth rate of 13%. What is India's PEG ratio? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: PEG = 20 ÷ 13 = 1.54. On these assumptions, India has the lowest PEG in the table despite having the highest P/E. But the result depends entirely on the growth assumption. If India's earnings grew only 10% a year, its PEG would be 2.0, no better than the US. The real question is not "Is India expensive?" but "Will India's earnings keep growing fast enough to justify the price?"

children.text: Tool 3: Look Through the Sector Mix

Every regional index is really a bundle of sectors, and sectors carry different valuations everywhere. Comparing index P/Es without looking at what is inside them is like comparing the average price of vehicles in two showrooms without checking whether one sells scooters and the other sells SUVs.

body.title: Which market feels interest rates most?
body.question: Based on sector mix, which two regional benchmarks are most directly exposed to the profitability of banks and financial companies?
body.explanation: Financials make up over a third of the Nifty 50 and about a quarter of MSCI Europe. Bank profits depend heavily on interest rates, loan growth and credit quality, so RBI and ECB decisions matter enormously for these indices. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 are dominated by technology, and the TAIEX and KOSPI by semiconductors.

children.text: Tool 4: Follow the Cash Returned to Shareholders

Your return from owning shares comes from two places: price gains and cash paid out. Markets return cash in different ways. Europe leans on dividends. The US leans on buybacks, which reduce the share count and lift earnings per share. Japan has turned to both as governance reforms push companies to stop hoarding cash. India's large companies pay relatively modest dividends and reinvest more, which makes sense when growth opportunities are plentiful.

children.text: For an Indian investor, a market's return in its own currency is only half the story. Over long periods, the rupee has generally weakened against the US dollar, which has boosted the rupee value of dollar investments. In mid-2026 the rupee traded around 95 per dollar. The same effect works in reverse for foreign investors in India: a falling rupee eats into their dollar returns, which is one reason FPIs watch the rupee as closely as the Nifty.

body.title: A dollar return in rupees
body.prompt: Illustrative figures: a US index fund returns 10% in a year in dollar terms, and the rupee weakens 3% against the dollar over the same year, so the dollar gains 3% in rupee terms. Using (1 + index return) × (1 + currency change) − 1, what is the return in rupees? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Return in ₹ = (1 + 0.10) × (1 + 0.03) − 1 = 1.10 × 1.03 − 1 = 1.133 − 1 = 13.3%. For a US investor in an Indian fund earning 13% in rupees while the rupee falls 3%, the dollar return would be 1.13 × 0.97 − 1 = 9.6%. Currency can quietly close most of the gap between two markets' headline returns.

body.title: Flip the ratio
body.textWithBlank: The earnings yield of a market is simply the inverse of its ___ ratio, expressed as a percentage.
body.explanation: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E × 100. A P/E of 25 gives an earnings yield of 4%, and a P/E of 12.5 gives 8%. Converting P/E into a yield makes it easy to compare shares with bonds and fixed deposits.

body.title: Picking "the best market"
body.scenario: Your cousin, a software engineer in Hyderabad, has ₹10 lakh to invest for 10 years. They say: "India is at 20 times earnings and the 10-year G-Sec pays 7.10%, so Indian stocks are overpriced. Europe is at 14.6 times, so I'll put everything in a European fund. Or maybe the US, because its earnings are growing fastest."
body.prompt: Using the five tools from this lesson, explain what your cousin should consider before choosing, and why putting everything in one region is risky.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Valuation: India's 20x is high and its yield gap against a 7.10% G-Sec is negative, so a lot of growth is priced in. Europe's 14.6x is lower, but that is partly explained by its sector mix and slower growth.
2. Growth: On a PEG basis, India can look reasonable if earnings grow around 13% a year for a long time. If growth disappoints, the high P/E is a risk. US earnings are strong now, but one boom year does not guarantee a decade.
3. Sector mix: The US is a technology bet, Europe and India are heavily financial, and Taiwan and Korea are chip bets. Choosing a region is really choosing a set of sectors.
4. Cash returned: Europe pays higher dividends, the US uses buybacks, and India reinvests more for growth.
5. Currency: A European or US fund adds currency risk. Over long periods, a weakening rupee has helped foreign assets, but that can change.

Why one region is risky: Japan's 34-year wait to regain its 1989 peak shows a single market can disappoint for decades. A sensible approach is to keep a core in India, where the goals and expenses are in rupees, and add some global diversification, keeping overseas investment rules and taxes under LRS in mind.

body.title: The five-question market comparison
steps: Valuation: What is the forward P/E, from which source and date, and how does it compare with the market's own history?
Bonds: What is the earnings yield, and how does it compare with the local 10-year government bond yield?
Growth: What long-term earnings growth is realistic, and what PEG does that imply?
Sector mix: Which sectors dominate the index, and am I really choosing a region or a sector?
Cash and currency: How much cash is returned to shareholders, and what could the currency do to my rupee return?

points: In 2026, India and the US traded at the highest valuations among major markets, at roughly 20x and 19x forward earnings, with Japan near 16x, Europe near 14.6x and emerging markets overall near 13.8x.
Convert P/E into an earnings yield and compare it with local bond yields. India's yield gap was about −2.15 points against a 7.10% G-Sec, and the US gap was about +0.20 points.
Growth justifies higher valuations only if it lasts. On an illustrative 13% long-term growth assumption, India's PEG of 1.54 looks reasonable despite its high P/E.
Sector mix drives regional valuations: the US is a tech bet, Europe and India lean on financials, and Taiwan and Korea are chip bets.
Markets return cash differently: dividends in Europe, buybacks in the US, both in reform-driven Japan, and more reinvestment in India.
Always calculate returns in rupees. Currency moves can add to or erase much of the gap between markets.
Use all five tools together. No single metric tells you which market will do best.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Valuation, yield, buyback and sector figures are drawn from FactSet, LSEG, MSCI, NSE, S&P Dow Jones Indices, Morningstar and published reports as of the dates stated, come from different sources and dates, and may change. Growth assumptions, PEG ratios and currency figures in the exercises are illustrative. Investing overseas from India is subject to LRS limits and tax rules. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any market or security.
